newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Math-minded gymnast ideal Mir repairman.
newsitem.headline: Math-minded gymnast ideal Mir repairman.

text.p: He was always "the other one", the unsung third man on the Mir space station -- until Friday when, working round the clock, engineer Alexander Lazutkin cranked the crippled ship back to life as his crewmates slept.

Few cosmonauts have had such a baptism of fire -- literally -- on their first mission. Lazutkin, an unassuming, moustachioed 39-year-old, had to deal with a serious blaze which broke out on the station within days of his arrival in February.

While scientific colleagues aboard have been frustrated by a series of mishaps, some of them nearly fatal, Lazutkin, with help from his crewmates and ground control, has pushed back the frontiers of human experience of emergency repair work in space.

If humankind goes on exploring the cosmos, then more astronauts will have to cope with the sort of repeated problems like fires and oxygen system breakdowns, leaks, collisions and computer crashes that "Sasha" Lazutkin has had to deal with.

His training as a competitive gymnast may have been as important for him as years working as an engineer at the Soviet Energia rocket company when it came to tackling long and arduous repairs aboard the 11-year-old Mir, which is showing its age.

It was Lazutkin, a married man with two children, who faced the most hazardous and demanding task following the June 25 accident when an unmanned craft being manoeuvred by Mir commander Vasily Tsibliyev collided with and punctured the Spektr module.

A meeting of Mission Control officials on Monday may decide to call the operation off and leave it to a relief crew next month. But for now Lazutkin is still scheduled to open the hatch into the now airless Spektr to repair severed electric cables.

Opening the hatch from an airlock between the module and the main Mir living area poses risks for the spacesuited cosmonaut who does it, since he has no way of knowing what possibly toxic, corrosive or sharp objects may be floating around inside.

Once inside, Lazutkin, backed by British-born NASA physicist Michael Foale after Tsibliyev withdrew with stress-induced heart trouble, would spend six to eight hours cramped up in a bulky spacesuit, painstakingly locating and splicing the jumble of wires connecting Spektr's solar panels to the main system.

One former astronaut described such an operation as being like "a very long workout" since, despite the lack of gravity in space, Lazutkin would have to fight with every movement of his joints against a build up of air pressure in the suit.
One person with no doubt about his ability to stand the strain is Oleg Grachev, head of Moscow's Olympic Sport School No. 51, where the cosmonaut was a budding teenage gymnast.
"He was a very disciplined," Grachev told Reuters. "Quiet, serious and always with his mind on his lessons."

Lazutkin would probably modestly agree with mission director Vladimir Solovyov's refusal to call him the hero of the day on Friday: "We only have heroes of the day on television. It was all in a day's work for the flight engineer."
